messages.subject: Difference between Stan estimates and those from moveHMM for an animal movement model
parts:
Hi,

I have been doing some work with animal movement models, and Bob kindly helped me out with coding this up in Stan (see code at bottom of this message.) I mentioned before in passing that I was seeing some differences in the estimates of the latent state from the R package 'moveHMM' and from my Stan model when using 'optimizing' to find the posterior modes. Since I am setting uniform priors on parameters, I figured that the results should be the same.

In this message I provide a working example to highlight the different results from each approach using fake data. (Was hoping this might help someone else in the future.)

Below I use the moveHMM package to generate the fake data (with an exponential step length distribution and a wrapped Cauchy angle distribution), then estimate the model,

library(moveHMM)
stepPar <- c(1,10) # mean1, mean2, sd1, sd2
anglePar <- c(0,0,0.3,0.7) # mean1, mean2, k1, k2
stepDist <- "exp"
angleDist <- "wrpcauchy"
beta <- t(c(-3,-3))

lTest <- simData(nbAnimals=1,nbStates=2,stepDist=stepDist,angleDist=angleDist,stepPar=stepPar,
                anglePar=anglePar,obsPerAnimal=1000,beta=beta,states = TRUE)
plot(lTest)

## Fit model, plot results and extract states
aFit <- fitHMM(data=lTest,nbStates = 2,stepDist=stepDist,angleDist=angleDist,stepPar=stepPar,
               anglePar=anglePar)
plot(aFit)
lStates <- viterbi(aFit)

## Determine correlation with true states
cor(lTest$states[-c(1,1000)],lStates[-c(1,1000)])

The correlation between the true state and the fitted is pretty good, usually above 0.95. If I do the same with my Stan code, I get different latent states. Note below I remove the first and last observations since Stan doesn't like NAs,

lTest_short <- lTest[-c(1,1000),]
fit <- optimizing(aModel,data=list(l=lTest_short$step,K=2,N=dim(lTest_short)[1],phi=lTest_short$angle))
lStates_MAP <- fit$par[11:1008]

And if I look at the correlation between these two it varies from run to run, but it barely gets above a magnitude of 0.6. The Stan model tends to get stuck in a state, meaning that it is not good at reproducing reality when there are rapid changes in the latent state.

Does anyone know why there might be this difference between the two approaches? Thanks!

functions{
  ## Function that returns the log pdf of the wrapped-Cauchy
  real wrappedCauchy(real aPhi, real aRho, real aMu) {
    return(- log(2*pi()) + log((1-aRho^2)/(1+aRho^2-2*aRho*cos(aPhi-aMu))));
  }
}

data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  vector<lower=-pi(), upper=pi()>[N] phi;
  vector<lower=0>[N] l;
  int<lower=1> K;
}

parameters {
  vector<lower=-pi(), upper=pi()>[K] mu;
  vector<lower=0,upper=1>[K] rho;
  positive_ordered[K] alpha;
  simplex[K] theta[K];
}  

model {
  vector[K] log_theta[K];
  vector[K] lp;

  for (k in 1:K) log_theta[k] = log(theta[k]);
  lp = rep_vector(-log(K), K); ## Initial state log-probability
  for (n in 1:N) {
    for (k in 1:K)
      lp[k]
        = log_sum_exp(log_theta[k] + lp)
        + wrappedCauchy(phi[n], rho[k], mu[k])
        + exponential_lpdf(l[n] | alpha[k]);
  }
  target += log_sum_exp(lp);
}

generated quantities {
  int<lower=1,upper=K> y_star[N];
  real log_p_y_star;
  {
    int back_ptr[N, K];
    real best_logp[N, K];
    real best_total_logp;
    for (k in 1:K)
      best_logp[1, K] = wrappedCauchy(phi[1], rho[k], mu[k])
                      + exponential_lpdf(l[1] | alpha[k]);
    for (t in 2:N) {
      for (k in 1:K) {
      best_logp[t, k] = negative_infinity();
        for (j in 1:K) {
          real logp;
          logp = best_logp[t-1, j]
          + log(theta[j, k]) + wrappedCauchy(phi[t], rho[k], mu[k])
                      + exponential_lpdf(l[t] | alpha[k]);
          if (logp > best_logp[t, k]) {
            back_ptr[t, k] = j;
            best_logp[t, k] = logp;
          }
        }
      }
    }
    log_p_y_star = max(best_logp[N]);
    for (k in 1:K)
      if (best_logp[N, k] == log_p_y_star)
      y_star[N] = k;
      for (t in 1:(N - 1))
      y_star[N - t] = back_ptr[N - t + 1,
      y_star[N - t + 1]];
  }
}

On Saturday, September 3, 2016 at 7:40:21 PM UTC-4, Ben Lambert wrote:
Does anyone know why there might be this difference between the two approaches? Thanks!

I do not, but one thing to try is to see if you get the same answer using optim() with method = "L-BFGS-B". Just create a stanfit object called sf by calling stan() with iter = 0 and then call optim() with
  • par = runif(get_num_upars(sf), min = -2, max = 2)
  • fn = log_prob
  • gr = grad_log_prob
  • ... as adjust_transform = FALSE and object = sf
  • method = "L-BFGS-B"
  • control = list(fnscale = -1)

That will separate differences between your Stan program and moveHMM from differences in how optimization works in Stan and R. There is nothing at all special about the optimizers in Stan except that they can utilize autodiff.


Ben

parts:
What's happening is that alpha[kk] is becoming zero at some
point. Are you sure the model has a mode with the
data you provide? Sometimes the likelihood can grow toward
a bound and cause underflow.

I'd suggest putting a prior on alpha[kk] that bounds it away
from zero like a lognormal().

Or you could try sampling rather than optimizing.

There are examples in the manual, too. You only need the
forward part of forward backward for Stan. If you use
all of forward-backward, you can often do analytical updates
of theta and weighted updates of the emission densities,
which would be faster, but is harder to code.

Also, your vectorization for log_theta was fine as it was
before but it'll be just as efficient with loops.

- Bob

This was my fault for giving you a buggy version of the
model in the first place. Sorry about that. I got too
excited after the conference in Seattle. Then didn't
pay enough attention to answering your email query.

Here's a model that works with von-Mises turns and Weibull
steps. You'll see that the theta matrix needs to be transposed,
then log_sum_exp-ed, because the forward algorithm adds all
the ways you can get from previous state to next state, so
that requires log_sum_exp (and the transposition, so the
simplex constraint is applied in the right place).


data {
int<lower=0> N;
vector<lower=-pi(), upper=pi()>[N] turn;
vector<lower=0>[N] dist;
int<lower=1> K;
}
parameters {
simplex[K] theta[K];
vector<lower=-pi(), upper=pi()>[K] mu;

vector<lower=0>[K] kappa;
positive_ordered[K] alpha;
vector<lower=0>[K] sigma;
}
model {
vector[K] log_theta_tr[K];
vector[K] lp;
vector[K] lp_p1;

for (k_from in 1:K)
for (k in 1:K)

log_theta_tr[k, k_from] = log(theta[k_from, k]);
lp = rep_vector(-log(K), K);
for (n in 1:N) {
for (k in 1:K)

lp_p1[k]
= log_sum_exp(log_theta_tr[k] + lp)
+ von_mises_lpdf(turn[n] | mu[k], kappa[k])
+ weibull_lpdf(dist[n] | alpha[k], sigma[k]);
lp = lp_p1;
}
target += log_sum_exp(lp);

kappa ~ lognormal(0, 2);
alpha ~ lognormal(0, 2);
sigma ~ lognormal(0, 1);
}

For the two-state HMM, I simulated

theta <- matrix(c(0.90, 0.10,
0.10, 0.90), 2, 2, byrow=TRUE);

mu <- c(-0.2, 0)
kappa <- c(0.5, 4)

alpha <- c(1, 3);
sigma <- c(0.25, 0.5);

and gave it a single 10,000-step simulated path. It converged
and fit fine in 200 iterations total in about 4 minutes and
recovered:

transitions are well estimated, but the locations of
the von Mises have fairly broad posteriors, which makes
sense given their wide scales.

do that with our unit_vector parameter type, but I
should be able to get that done for a case study (a

can then be translated back to an angle---all this trig

Hi Bob,

Please don't apologise -- I am very grateful to the time you personally have given me on this forum (I know I take more than most.) Also thanks very much for the new code -- looks pretty good!

I have now implemented the forwards-backwards algorithm (I think) and seem to be getting reasonable performance. The correlation between the estimated state and the true state is about 0.94. This is a bit lower than the moveHMM package estimates (a correlation of 0.97), but not far off.

Suspect there may be a small error in the code somewhere, but this isn't doing too badly. I have changed the step dist to an exponential since this is more in line with my data, but otherwise your code remains intact.

If anyone gets the chance to look through the below and comment on whether I'm making a silly mistake somewhere, then let me know. 

Best,

Ben

data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  vector<lower=-pi(), upper=pi()>[N] turn;
  vector<lower=0>[N] dist;
  int<lower=1> K;
}
parameters {
  simplex[K] theta[K];
  vector<lower=-pi(), upper=pi()>[K] mu;
  vector<lower=0>[K] kappa;
  positive_ordered[K] alpha;
}

transformed parameters {
  vector[K] log_theta_tr[K];

for (k_from in 1:K)
    for (k in 1:K)
      log_theta_tr[k, k_from] = log(theta[k_from, k]);
}
model {

vector[K] lp;
  vector[K] lp_p1;

lp = rep_vector(-log(K), K);
  
  # Forwards algorithm

for (n in 1:N) {
    for (k in 1:K){
      lp_p1[k]
        = log_sum_exp(log_theta_tr[k] + lp)
        + von_mises_lpdf(turn[n] | mu[k], kappa[k])
+ exponential_lpdf(dist[n] | alpha[k]);

}
    lp = lp_p1;
  }
  target += log_sum_exp(lp);
}

generated quantities{
  matrix[N,K] B;
  vector[K] lp_pTotal;
  vector[K] lp_p2;
  vector[K] lp_p1a;
  vector[K] lp_a;
  matrix[N,K] A;
  matrix[N,K] qState;
  vector[N] pState;
  
  # Forwards algorithm
  lp_a = rep_vector(-log(K), K);
for (n in 1:N) {

for (k in 1:K){
      lp_p1a[k]
        = log_sum_exp(log_theta_tr[k] + lp_a)
+ von_mises_lpdf(turn[n] | mu[k], kappa[k])

+ exponential_lpdf(dist[n] | alpha[k]);
    }
    lp_a = lp_p1a;
    A[n] = to_row_vector(lp_a);
  }
  
  ## Backwards algorithm http://www.cs.columbia.edu/~mcollins/fb.pdf
  B[N] = rep_row_vector(1,K);
  lp_pTotal = rep_vector(0,K);
  
  for(n in 1:(N-1)){
   for(k in 1:K){
     lp_p2[k]
        = log_sum_exp(log_theta_tr[k] + lp_pTotal)
        + von_mises_lpdf(turn[N - n + 1] | mu[k], kappa[k])
        + exponential_lpdf(dist[N - n + 1] | alpha[k]);
   } 
   lp_pTotal = lp_p2;
   B[N - n] = to_row_vector(lp_pTotal);
  }
  
  ## Estimate unnormalised state probs
  for(n in 1:N){
    for(k in 1:K){
      qState[n,k] = A[n,k] + B[n,k];
    }
  }
 
  # Normalise these to find prob of state 2 (am using a 2 state model)
  for(n in 1:N){
      pState[n] = exp(qState[n,2] - log_sum_exp(qState[n]));
  }
}

I have made a look at the moveHMM package -- they use the viterbi algorithm to compute the most likely sequence of states, rather than forwards-backwards (see https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/moveHMM/vignettes/moveHMM-guide.pdf). 

This is the right thing to do, it seems. The forwards-backwards can compute the most likely individual state for any given point in time, whereas the viterbi is what we want to use if we want to compute the most likely sequence of states (see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forward%E2%80%93backward_algorithm). The differences between these two is quite subtle!

When I replace the forwards-backwards code (in the 'generated quantities' section) with the viterbi I get the same performance as moveHMM in estimating the state probabilities! Looks like all is working now, thanks again,

generated quantities {
  int<lower=1,upper=K> y_star[N];
  real log_p_y_star;
  {
    int back_ptr[N, K];
    real best_logp[N, K];
    real best_total_logp;
for (k in 1:K)

best_logp[1, K] = von_mises_lpdf(turn[1] | mu[k], kappa[k])
                      + exponential_lpdf(dist[1] | alpha[k]);
    for (t in 2:N) {
for (k in 1:K) {

best_logp[t, k] = negative_infinity();
        for (j in 1:K) {
          real logp;
          logp = best_logp[t-1, j]

+ log(theta[j, k]) + von_mises_lpdf(turn[t] | mu[k], kappa[k])
                      + exponential_lpdf(dist[t] | alpha[k]);

if (logp > best_logp[t, k]) {
            back_ptr[t, k] = j;
            best_logp[t, k] = logp;
          }
        }
      }
    }
    log_p_y_star = max(best_logp[N]);
for (k in 1:K)

if (best_logp[N, k] == log_p_y_star)
      y_star[N] = k;
      for (t in 1:(N - 1))
      y_star[N - t] = back_ptr[N - t + 1,
      y_star[N - t + 1]];
  }
}

parts:
Glad to hear the performance is the same.

The Viterbi algorithm finds the most probable state sequence z*
given the observed data y (emissions) and parameters theta
(transition and distributions of emissions per state):

z* = ARGMAX_z p(z | y, theta)

whereas forward-backward computes the marginal probability
that state z[t] = k, given the observed data and parameters

Pr[z[t] = k | y, theta]

You can use that to find the most likely state at time t,
but that's not necessarily the same as z*[t].

With forward backward and a little more work, you can compute
the probabitity of any subsequence of states. And with Viterbi,
you can generalize to output the N-best possible sequences in
order.

- Bob

parts:
Yes, I have been using the state probabilities for the last training set observation to initialise my forward algorithm on the test set. (Rather than in the full forward where we assign equal probability to each state initially.) 

This means that I use the forwards-backwards algorithm on the training set to determine the state probabilities for the last observation. I then use these to initialise a forward run on the test set. This means that I do the following and use ``lp_testOverall'' to measure the out-of-sample predictive capability of the model,

generated quantities{
  matrix[N,K] B;
  vector[K] lp_pTotal;
  vector[K] lp_p2;
  vector[K] lp_p1a;
  vector[K] lp_a;
  matrix[N,K] A;
  matrix[N,K] qState;
  vector[N] pState;

matrix[N,K] pStateAll;
  
  ## Test sample
  vector[K] lp_test;
  vector[K] lp_testTemp;
  real lp_testOverall;

# Forwards algorithm
  lp_a = rep_vector(-log(K), K);
  
  for (n in 1:N) {
    for (k in 1:K){
      lp_p1a[k]
        = log_sum_exp(log_theta_tr[k] + lp_a)
+ wrappedCauchy(turn[n] , rho[k], mu[k])

+ exponential_lpdf(dist[n] | alpha[k]);
    }
    lp_a = lp_p1a;
    A[n] = to_row_vector(lp_a);
  }
  
  
  ## Backwards algorithm http://www.cs.columbia.edu/~mcollins/fb.pdf
  B[N] = rep_row_vector(1,K);
  lp_pTotal = rep_vector(0,K);
  
  for(n in 1:(N-1)){
   for(k in 1:K){
     lp_p2[k]
        = log_sum_exp(log_theta_tr[k] + lp_pTotal)
+ wrappedCauchy(turn[N - n + 1] , rho[k], mu[k])

+ exponential_lpdf(dist[N - n + 1] | alpha[k]);
   } 
   lp_pTotal = lp_p2;
   B[N - n] = to_row_vector(lp_pTotal);
  }
  
  ## Estimate unnormalised state probs
  for(n in 1:N){
    for(k in 1:K){
      qState[n,k] = A[n,k] + B[n,k];
    }
  }
  
  # Normalise these to find prob of state 2 (am using a 2 state model)
  for(n in 1:N){
      pState[n] = exp(qState[n,2] - log_sum_exp(qState[n]));

pStateAll[n] = exp(qState[n] - log_sum_exp(qState[n]));
  }
  
  # Out-of-sample predictive capability estimation

  ## Initialise state probs according to last training set obs
  lp_test = to_vector(pStateAll[N]);

 ## Use forward algorithm 
  for (n in 1:N1) {
    for (k in 1:K){
      lp_testTemp[k]
        = log_sum_exp(log_theta_tr[k] + lp_test)
        + wrappedCauchy(turnTest[n] , rho[k], mu[k])
        + exponential_lpdf(distTest[n] | alpha[k]);
    }
    lp_test = lp_testTemp;
  }
  ### sum over X_k to marginalise
  lp_testOverall = log_sum_exp(lp_test);
  
}

parts:
Just in case someone will find this useful for future work, I have now extended the model to allow for covariates to affect the probability of switching states. Specifically, I have used the same framework explained in https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/moveHMM/vignettes/moveHMM-guide.pdf, on pages 19 and 20, where the off-diagonal probabilities are multinomial logits.

The below seems to reproduce the parameters that I use to generate the data, and be in line with the states estimated via fitHMM itself. Note: I have checked the model only for the 2- and 3-state models, with a single covariate. 

Does anyone think that it'd be worthwhile added functionality to Stan that implements estimation of these animal movement HMMs? That is, rather than the user having to code them up as I've done below. As a starter it might be good to try to add the distributions and models from the moveHMM package. Could always extend to more general HMMs later.

Best, Ben

functions{
  ## Function that returns the log pdf of the wrapped-Cauchy
  real wrappedCauchy(real aPhi, real aRho, real aMu) {
    return(- log(2*pi()) + log((1-aRho^2)/(1+aRho^2-2*aRho*cos(aPhi-aMu))));
  }

## Function that returns a random sample from wrapped-Cauchy by first
  ## sampling from the Cauchy, then using modular arithmetic
  real wrappedCauchy_rng(real aRho, real aMu){
    real aCauchyRand;
    real aWCRand;
    
    aCauchyRand = cauchy_rng(pi()+aMu,-log(aRho));
    if (aCauchyRand>0){
      aWCRand = fmod(aCauchyRand,2*pi()) - pi();
    } else{
      aWCRand = -fmod(-aCauchyRand,2*pi()) + pi();   
    }

    return(aWCRand);

}
  
}

data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  vector<lower=-pi(), upper=pi()>[N] turn;
  vector<lower=0>[N] dist;
  int<lower=1> K;

## Out-of-sample test
  int N1;
  vector<lower=-pi(), upper=pi()>[N1] turnTest;
  vector<lower=0>[N1] distTest;
  
  # Covariate
  int nCovs;
  matrix[N,nCovs+1] X;
}

parameters {
vector<lower=-pi(), upper=pi()>[K] mu;

vector<lower=0,upper=1>[K] rho;
  positive_ordered[K] alpha;

matrix[K*(K-1),nCovs+1] beta;
}

transformed parameters {
  ## Gamma here is a matrix of the log probabilities not probabilities as in the moveHMM doc
  matrix[K,K] Gamma[N];
  matrix[K,K] Gamma_tr[N];
  
  for(n in 1:N){
    int aCount;
    aCount = 1;
    for(k_from in 1:K){
      for(k in 1:K){
        if(k_from==k){
          Gamma[n,k_from,k] = 1;
      }else{
          Gamma[n,k_from,k] = exp(beta[aCount] * to_vector(X[n]));
          aCount = aCount + 1;
      }
    }
    }
    Gamma[n] = log(Gamma[n]/sum(Gamma[n]));
  }
  
  for(n in 1:N)
    for(k_from in 1:K)
      for(k  in 1:K)
        Gamma_tr[n, k, k_from] = Gamma[n,k_from,k];

}

model {
  vector[K] lp;
  vector[K] lp_p1;
  
  lp = rep_vector(-log(K), K);
  
  # Forwards algorithm
  for (n in 1:N) {
    for (k in 1:K){
      lp_p1[k]
= log_sum_exp(to_vector(Gamma_tr[n,k]) + lp)

+ wrappedCauchy(turn[n] , rho[k], mu[k])
        + exponential_lpdf(dist[n] | alpha[k]);
    }

lp = lp_p1;
  }
  target += log_sum_exp(lp);

}

generated quantities{

## Viterbi to estimate most likely state vector
  int<lower=1,upper=K> state[N];

real log_p_y_star;
  {
    int back_ptr[N, K];
    real best_logp[N, K];
    real best_total_logp;
    for (k in 1:K)
best_logp[1, K] = wrappedCauchy(turn[1] , rho[k], mu[k])

+ exponential_lpdf(dist[1] | alpha[k]);
    for (t in 2:N) {
      for (k in 1:K) {
      best_logp[t, k] = negative_infinity();
        for (j in 1:K) {
          real logp;
          logp = best_logp[t-1, j]
+ Gamma[t,j,k] + wrappedCauchy(turn[t] , rho[k], mu[k])

+ exponential_lpdf(dist[t] | alpha[k]);
          if (logp > best_logp[t, k]) {
            back_ptr[t, k] = j;
            best_logp[t, k] = logp;
          }
        }
      }
    }
    log_p_y_star = max(best_logp[N]);
    for (k in 1:K)
      if (best_logp[N, k] == log_p_y_star)
state[N] = k;
for (t in 1:(N - 1))

state[N - t] = back_ptr[N - t + 1,
      state[N - t + 1]];
  }
}
